Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search); a fresh install seeds the last 30 days from Settings → Dashboard Data → Run backfill. The global Cloud dropdown filters the summaries through the cloud_provider dimension stored in every rollup row. Full schedule and freshness reference: Performance & Data Freshness.

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
• Firewall drop spikes – A sudden increase in Firewall Drops at Host may indicate port scanning, network reconnaissance, or a brute-force attack against SAP services.
  • Top Drop Source concentration – If the Top Drop Source KPI shows a single IP accounting for the overwhelming majority of drops, that IP is either a misconfigured internal system hammering a blocked port (check if it’s an internal SAP host that recently changed config) or a persistent external scanner. The Blocked Sources table below has the full ranking, and its At Host and In Transit / Other columns show whether that source was reaching the host itself or systems the host routes to.
  • Drops in transit – Only a host that routes traffic onward, such as a VPN or IPsec gateway, logs FWD_DROP. On a gateway, drops in transit are traffic its forwarding policy does not allow, often a monitoring or discovery job pinging or probing the systems behind it, and they can outnumber the drops at the host many times over. Find the source in the Blocked Sources table and the job that owns it, then either allow that traffic or stop the job. Drops in transit on a host that is not meant to route at all mean IP forwarding is switched on there (container runtimes and Kubernetes nodes do this) and deserve a look.
  • New blocked source IPs – Unfamiliar source IPs appearing in the Blocked Sources table should be investigated, especially if they target SAP service ports (3200-3299 for dialog, 8000-8099 for HTTP, 30015 for HANA).
  • SAP application distribution changes – If the SAP Application Activity chart shows a previously active SID or application going silent, it may indicate a process crash or configuration issue.
  • OOM kills and soft lockups – The OOM Kills panels and CPU Soft Lockups table are the crash-adjacent signals on this dashboard: a process repeatedly targeted by the OOM killer, or recurring soft lockups on one host, may affect SAP system stability.
  • Port targeting patterns – The Blocked Destination Ports table reveals which services attackers are targeting. Ports associated with SAP services warrant immediate attention.

docs.title: Why This Dashboard Matters
docs.text:
The Multi-Cloud Overview dashboard answers the question: “Where is our LogServ data coming from, and is it balanced between cloud providers?” It splits ingest by the indexed cloud_provider field so admins running any mix of AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, and Google Cloud Storage ingest can confirm each pipeline is healthy and see relative volume at a glance.

Customers running a single cloud see the dashboard collapse cleanly to one provider (the unused providers’ KPIs show 0, the active provider’s series carries the trend chart). Customers running two or three clouds — common during a migration or in a multi-region SAP landscape — see comparative KPIs + side-by-side trend so they can spot a stalled ingest channel before it becomes a visible gap in their other operational dashboards.

How cloud_provider is attributed

Azure-sourced events carry an indexed cloud_provider = azure field, set by the Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure add-on’s sap_logserv_azure_queue input stanza via _meta = cloud_provider::azure; GCP-sourced events likewise carry cloud_provider = gcp via the Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP add-on’s sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input (_meta = cloud_provider::gcp) — both add-ons inject the setting automatically. Legacy AWS events without the field are defaulted to aws at search time via the sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro (eval cloud_provider=coalesce(cloud_provider, "aws")). Every panel on this dashboard applies the macro so the per-provider split is always meaningful regardless of when the events landed. To attribute new AWS events explicitly at ingest time (recommended for any new HF rollout), set _meta = cloud_provider::aws on your Splunk_TA_aws SQS-based S3 input stanzas — see the Azure Setup Guide / GCP Setup Guide for the full configuration pattern (the same pattern applies symmetrically to every cloud). Alternatively, the LogServ Data TA’s Configuration → Cloud Provider dropdown (AWS / Microsoft Azure / Google Cloud Platform / Not set) stamps cloud_provider on every event the TA processes — the simpler, TA-managed option for a Heavy Forwarder that ingests from a single cloud. See Configuring Filters → Cloud Provider Attribution.

docs.title: Panels
docs.text:
• Total Events – Aggregate event count across ALL ingest channels with a daily-volume sparkline. Useful as the baseline for comparing the per-provider KPIs that follow.
  • AWS Events – Event count where cloud_provider = "aws" (includes events explicitly attributed at ingest time AND legacy events defaulted via the macro). Sparkline shows daily AWS-only volume.
  • Azure Events – Event count where cloud_provider = "azure". Sparkline shows daily Azure-only volume. On an install without Azure ingest, this KPI shows 0 and its sparkline is empty.
  • GCP Events – Event count where cloud_provider = "gcp". Sparkline shows daily GCP-only volume. On an install without GCP ingest, this KPI shows 0 and its sparkline is empty.
  • Event Volume by Cloud Provider – Stacked column chart showing event counts over time, split by provider. Each bar is one time bucket’s total; the per-provider segments stack to make each contribution visible. Useful for spotting shifts over time (a sudden drop in one provider’s stack height while the others stay flat = that provider’s ingest stalled).
  • Event Count by Provider – One-row-per-provider table with the raw cumulative event counts. The same data as the per-provider KPIs but in tabular form so the ratios are easy to read.
  • Distinct Hosts by Provider – One-row-per-provider table showing how many unique host values reported under each cloud_provider. Confirms forwarder coverage across the cloud boundary.
  • Distinct Sourcetypes by Provider – One-row-per-provider table showing how many distinct sourcetypes have at least one event per provider. Useful for confirming every cloud is producing the full sourcetype mix (e.g., not just linux_messages_syslog from Azure while AWS has the SAP stack).
  • About the cloud_provider field – Inline reference panel (not a search result) explaining how the field is set + linking to the Azure and GCP Setup Guides. Always visible as a customer-friendly reminder of the attribution mechanic.
  • Top Sourcetypes by Cloud Provider – Wide table of the 30 most-active sourcetypes with per-provider columns (AWS Events / Azure Events / GCP Events / Total). The Total column is sorted descending so the high-volume sourcetypes lead. Useful for spotting per-sourcetype anomalies (e.g., sap:hana:audit is only appearing under one cloud when several should be producing it).

docs.title: Where the Data Comes From
docs.text:
Panels read the logserv_mc_rollup KV Store collection — metric count carries per-hour event counts by (cloud provider, sourcetype) and metric hosts the per-provider host sets (kept separate so distinct-host counts stay correct when an event carries a multivalue host). Populated at minute :22 of every hour by logserv_mc_aggregate over the entire index, keyed on the cloud_provider indexed field stamped at ingest (see Required Configuration below); events with no provider attribution are counted as aws by convention.

Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search); a fresh install seeds the last 30 days from Settings → Dashboard Data → Run backfill. Unlike the other dashboards, this one is exempt from the global Cloud dropdown — its panels pin their own provider values (AWS / Azure / GCP side by side), so a global filter would be circular. Full schedule and freshness reference: Performance & Data Freshness.

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
• Stalled ingest channel – If one provider’s KPI sparkline goes flat-zero for the most recent 1–3 days while the others continue to climb, the affected channel’s input has likely stalled. Check the LogServ Azure add-on’s sap_logserv_azure_queue input on the Heavy Forwarder (per-firing summary in splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure_queue.log: Input '<name>' done: messages=N blobs=N events=N ...), the LogServ GCP add-on’s sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub input (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub.log: Input '<name>' done: messages=N objects=N events=N ...), or the Splunk_TA_aws S3 input for AWS (the S3Input component in index=_internal sourcetype=splunkd).
  • Asymmetric sourcetype coverage – If both clouds report comparable total event counts but the Top Sourcetypes table shows one cloud with a narrow sourcetype mix (e.g., AWS only producing sap:hana:audit while Azure produces 25+ sourcetypes), the AWS-side filter rules may be set to include-only rather than include-all. Check the Configure Filters page.
  • Unexpected appearance of aws from an Azure- or GCP-only customer – If your environment has no AWS ingest but the AWS Events KPI shows non-zero values, it likely means some legacy events that pre-date the cloud_provider field landed without explicit attribution and the macro defaulted them to aws. This is benign for trend-reporting (the events are still real), but to keep the labeling accurate you can stamp those legacy events via a one-time backfill or simply let them age out per index retention.
  • Distinct Hosts count substantially lower than expected – If a single cloud’s “Distinct Hosts” count is much lower than the actual count of SAP hosts in that cloud, your add-on input config may be too narrow (wrong container prefix on the Azure side, wrong subscription on the GCP side, wrong bucket prefix on the AWS side). Compare against your topology source-of-truth.
  • Total Events ≠ sum of the per-provider KPIs – Total Events counts every event regardless of cloud_provider value, while the three per-provider KPIs match aws / azure / gcp exactly. If Total exceeds their sum, some events carry a different cloud_provider value — run | tstats count WHERE `sap_logserv_idx_macro` BY cloud_provider to see it. If instead the AWS KPI under-reports, check that the sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro macro (which defaults legacy un-attributed events to aws) is loaded in your search head’s macros.conf — the LogServ App ships it in default/macros.conf; confirm with | rest /services/configs/conf-macros | search title=sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro.

docs.title: Drill-Down Behavior
docs.text:
Every KPI sparkline and the Event Volume by Cloud Provider chart respect the dashboard’s global time-range picker + the per-dashboard Refresh picker like any other LogServ App dashboard. Unlike other dashboards, this one has no Cloud Provider picker in its title row — the provider split is the dashboard, so every panel reports all providers side by side.

Tables on this dashboard are inventory views — they don’t yet wire click-to-drill-down behavior (because the natural drill destination would be a Splunk search filtered by cloud_provider which most customers will see directly via the macro on any dashboard).

docs.title: Required Configuration
docs.text:
This dashboard works out of the box on any LogServ App install (it gracefully shows 0 for unused providers), but the data quality is governed by the upstream ingest config:

  1. For Azure ingest: the _meta = cloud_provider::azure line is present on the [sap_logserv_azure_queue://...] stanza automatically (the LogServ Azure add-on injects it). See Azure Setup Guide.
  2. For GCP ingest: the _meta = cloud_provider::gcp line is present on the [sap_logserv_gcp_pubsub://...] stanza automatically (the LogServ GCP add-on injects it). See GCP Setup Guide.
  3. For explicit AWS attribution (optional): either set the LogServ Data TA’s Configuration → Cloud Provider dropdown to AWS (stamps cloud_provider = aws on every event the TA processes — simplest for a single-cloud Heavy Forwarder), OR add _meta = cloud_provider::aws to each [aws_sqs_based_s3://<your input name>] stanza in Splunk_TA_aws’s local/inputs.conf (use this per-input form when one HF ingests from more than one cloud). Without either, AWS events get the value via the search-time sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro macro — still correct for this dashboard, but the field is not indexed which means it can’t be used as a filter on raw-event searches outside this dashboard’s macro-wrapped panels. See Configuring Filters → Cloud Provider Attribution.
  4. Macro must be present: the LogServ App’s default/macros.conf defines [sap_logserv_cloud_provider_default_macro] with definition = eval cloud_provider=coalesce(cloud_provider, "aws"). If you’ve overridden macros.conf in your local app directory, ensure this macro is still defined.

See the Azure Setup Guide and the GCP Setup Guide for the canonical setup procedures (including the cloud_provider attribution pattern that applies symmetrically to every cloud).

docs.title: Why This Dashboard Matters
docs.text: The Proxy Analytics dashboard monitors outbound internet access through the Squid proxy server. In SAP environments, proxy logs reveal which systems and users are accessing external resources, enabling detection of data exfiltration attempts, policy violations (unauthorized internet access), and compromised systems communicating with malicious infrastructure. Proxy logs complement DNS analytics by showing the actual HTTP connections that follow DNS resolution.

docs.title: Panels
docs.text:
• Total Requests – Aggregate proxy request count
  • Total Bandwidth – Sum of bytes transferred through the proxy (formatted KB/MB/GB)
  • Denied Requests – Count of requests blocked by proxy policy
  • Request Volume Over Time – Request trend over time
  • Status Code Distribution – Stacked column chart of response categories (2xx-5xx)
  • Domains – Table of the most accessed domains with request counts, bandwidth, and unique client counts
  • Clients – Table of the most active client IPs with request counts, bandwidth, and domain diversity
  • Clients by Domain Diversity – Table ranking client IPs by the count of distinct URL domains they accessed. Click a row to open Host Details for that client (replaces the earlier HTTP Methods donut, which consistently collapsed to a single slice and didn’t earn its space)
  • Cache Action Distribution – Table of Squid cache/result actions (vendor_action, e.g. TCP_TUNNEL, TCP_HIT, TCP_MISS, TCP_DENIED, TCP_TUNNEL_ABORTED) ranked by event count – replaces the earlier Content Types donut for the same single-slice reason and reveals cache-hit behavior
  • Bandwidth Over Time – Column chart of total bytes out over time
  • URL Domains by Bytes Out – Table of URL domains ranked by MB delivered (the data-exfiltration detection surface); paginated, not capped. Click a row for that domain’s full proxy log
  • Bandwidth Over Time by Domain (Top 5) – Stacked column chart of the five highest-bandwidth domains over time – pairs with URL Domains by Bytes Out to show whether exfiltration is ongoing or historical
  • Slowest Destinations – Top destinations by peak response time, with request count and average/max latency (ms), from the Squid duration field
  • Response Time (Avg / Max) – Average and peak proxy response time over time

docs.title: Where the Data Comes From
docs.text:
The single source is squid:access, and only its access-log lines count as requests. The Data TA routes Squid’s cache.log and store.log to squid:cache and squid:store, but data indexed before that change carries them as squid:access, where they record cache housekeeping, not requests, so every panel scopes to source="*access.log*". Both access-log formats are parsed: Squid’s native format, and the logformat=splunk_recommended_squid key=value format that SAP LogServ proxy logs use (from build 364; earlier builds extracted no fields from it).

  • Summary-backed panels read the logserv_proxy_rollup KV Store collection — metrics core (per-hour request/denied/bandwidth sums), status (HTTP status classes), dur + destdur (response-time sums/counts/maxima overall and per destination — the Avg/Max panels reconstruct exact averages from these), domain (per-domain traffic and bandwidth) and cacheaction (Squid cache verdicts). Populated at minute :24 of every hour by logserv_proxy_aggregate.
  • Pure-count panels run tstats directly against indexed fields.

Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search); a fresh install seeds the last 30 days from Settings → Dashboard Data → Run backfill. The global Cloud dropdown filters the summaries through the cloud_provider dimension stored in every rollup row. Full schedule and freshness reference: Performance & Data Freshness.

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
• Denied request spikes – A sudden increase in denied requests may indicate a compromised system attempting to reach blocked destinations, or a policy change affecting legitimate traffic.
  • High-bandwidth domains – The URL Domains by Bytes Out panel is tuned specifically for exfiltration detection. A new domain appearing near the top, or a known-OK domain spiking, warrants investigation.
  • Sustained-bandwidth domains – The Bandwidth Over Time by Domain chart shows whether a top domain’s traffic is steady (expected service) or a sudden burst (exfiltration attempt, large file transfer).
  • Client domain diversity – A client IP with extremely high domain diversity in the Clients by Domain Diversity panel is unusual for a well-behaved SAP server – most production systems talk to a predictable small set of external domains.
  • Cache miss dominance – If Cache Action Distribution is dominated by TCP_MISS, the proxy cache may not be earning its keep (or a new workload is defeating it). For security-relevant investigations, TCP_TUNNEL dominance signals mostly CONNECT-tunnelled HTTPS traffic that the proxy can’t inspect.
  • New high-volume clients – A system that suddenly appears as a top proxy client may be compromised and performing outbound scanning, beaconing, or data exfiltration.

Squid parsing is built into the LogServ App

The App absorbed the native-format parsing from the archived Splunk Add-on for Squid Proxy, and parses the splunk_recommended_squid format with its own transforms. Do not install the standalone Squid TA alongside it — you would get double parsing, and its CIM-standard action="blocked" vocabulary differs from the App’s customized action="denied", which the Denied Requests KPI and the Cache Action panel depend on. The App shows a detection banner on the home view when a conflicting add-on is enabled.

docs.title: Why This Dashboard Matters
docs.text:
The Windows Events dashboard monitors Windows hosts in the SAP landscape, which commonly run SAP application servers, database instances, and management consoles. Windows Event Logs capture service health, PowerShell execution, and system errors that indicate Windows-specific operational issues. This dashboard focuses on operational health and service state – the authentication-failure story is owned by the Cross-Stack Authentication dashboard so that all three layers (SAP / HANA / Windows) can be investigated together.

Requires the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows on the Search Head

Several panels here depend on the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742) being installed on the Search Head tier. The LogServ App ships no XmlWinEventLog field extraction of its own — EventCode and severity are search-time fields provided by add-on 742 (its xmlwindows_severities.csv lookup maps the event <Level> to severity: 1→critical, 2→high, 3→medium, 0/4/5→informational).

Without add-on 742 on the search tier, Windows events still index fine and the Total Events, Event Volume by Log, Active Hosts, and PowerShell Activity panels populate (they read envelope fields), but the Event Codes table collapses to a single row labelled (none) and the Severity Distribution, Critical / Error, and Service Events panels stay empty.

Tier matters: EventCode/severity are search-time extractions, so add-on 742 must be on the Search Head — installing it on a Heavy Forwarder or indexer does nothing for these panels. On Splunk Cloud, install it on the Cloud SH via self-service app management (it is replicated to the indexer search peers through the knowledge bundle). After installing it, re-run the Windows and Environment Health rollups (Settings → Dashboard Data → Run backfill) so the cached panels pick up the now-extracted fields. See the Quick Install Reference package matrix.

docs.title: Panels
docs.text:
• Total Events – Aggregate Windows event count
  • Critical / Error – Count of Windows Critical (Level 1) and Error (Level 2) events. In CIM severity vocabulary these are severity="critical" and severity="high" — there is no error severity value
  • Active Hosts – Count of distinct Windows hosts reporting data
  • Event Volume by Log – Trend over time by Windows log source (Application, Security, System, PowerShell)
  • Severity Distribution Over Time – Stacked column chart of severity levels
  • Event Codes – Featured full-width table of the most frequent EventCodes with 7 enriched columns: Event Code, Description (signature), Source log, Severity, Events, Hosts (distinct count), Last Seen. Row drilldown opens the search app filtered by that event code.
  • Service Events – Table of Windows service start/stop activity with latest state
  • PowerShell Activity – Column chart of PowerShell operational event volume over time

docs.title: Where the Data Comes From
docs.text:
The single source is XmlWinEventLog. Every panel is summary-backed: panels read the logserv_windows_rollup KV Store collection — metric main carries an hourly grain over (event code, severity, source/channel, host) plus per-bucket latest values for the descriptive columns, and metric svc carries the service-event facts. Populated at minute :20 of every hour by logserv_windows_aggregate.

Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search); a fresh install seeds the last 30 days from Settings → Dashboard Data → Run backfill. The global Cloud dropdown filters the summaries through the cloud_provider dimension stored in every rollup row. Full schedule and freshness reference: Performance & Data Freshness.

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
• High-frequency Event Codes – The Event Codes table is the primary starting point. EventCode 7031 / 7034 (service terminated unexpectedly), 1000 (application crash), and 41 (unexpected shutdown) are high-priority. Click through to see every occurrence of a specific code.
  • Service crashes – EventCode 7031 (service terminated unexpectedly) in either the Event Codes table or the Service Events panel indicates a critical service failure. For SAP services (sapstartsrv, SAPService), this requires immediate attention.
  • PowerShell activity spikes – Sudden increases in PowerShell execution may indicate lateral movement by an attacker using PowerShell-based attack tools. Correlate with the Cross-Stack Authentication dashboard to see whether any Windows logons were concurrent.
  • Critical/error severity trends – A rising trend in critical and error events over multiple days indicates accumulating system health issues that need proactive investigation.
  • Event Code hosts expanding – The Hosts column on the Event Codes table makes it obvious when a normally-host-isolated error starts appearing on multiple hosts – a sign the underlying cause is environmental (failed update, domain policy change) rather than local.

docs.title: Why This Dashboard Matters
docs.text: Compliance conversations (SOX, PCI, internal change management) all require evidence that configuration changes are (1) authorized, (2) attributable to a specific operator, and (3) happening in approved maintenance windows. That evidence lives scattered across three audit trails: HANA audit logs (user/role/privilege/password operations and DDL), Windows Security Event Log (account and group modifications), and Linux syslog (sudo commands plus useradd/usermod/userdel/passwd events). This dashboard unifies the three into a single audit trail with a consistent operator column and category taxonomy, plus two compliance-focused “recent” tables: one filtered to privileged actions, one filtered to after-hours activity.

docs.title: Panels
docs.text:
Leave the Cloud Provider picker on All for compliance reporting

The title row carries the app-wide Cloud Provider picker. Any setting other than All silently narrows the audit trail to one ingest channel — for compliance evidence, always leave it on All.

  • Total Change Events – Aggregate count of change events across all three sources
  • User Account Changes – Count of user-management actions (HANA User Management/User Creation/User Deletion; Windows EventCodes 4720/4722/4725/4726/4738/4781; Linux useradd/usermod/userdel)
  • Permission Grants – Count of privilege/group-membership grants (HANA Permission Grant; Windows EventCodes 4728/4732/4756 – “added to group”)
  • Password Events – Count of password changes and resets (HANA Password Management/Password Reset; Windows EventCode 4724; Linux passwd)
  • After-Hours Changes (orange when non-zero) – Count of change events occurring outside business hours (weekday 8am-7pm, i.e. 08:00-18:59) or on weekends, judged in your own time zone (your Splunk time-zone preference). All three sources use the same window, and the KPI, its sparkline and the After-Hours table agree whichever path serves them
  • Unique Operators – Distinct count of source-prefixed operator identities (e.g., HANA:XCPADM, Windows:domain\admin, Linux:ops-user)
  • Change Activity Over Time (by Source) – Stacked column over time, its bucket size named in the subtitle (left half of the row, beside the Category donut), series split by source (HANA / Windows / Linux). Same-day spikes across two or three series often line up with maintenance windows; isolated spikes in one source worth investigating.
  • Change Events by Category – Donut showing the category mix: Permission Grant, Permission Revoke, User Management, Password Change, Group Membership, Account Status, Sudo Command, DDL / Config, Other.
  • Operators by Change Count (Source-Prefixed) – Full-width table of operator identities across all three stacks ranked by change events (paginated), with source-prefixed identities so operator activity is clearly scoped to each system.
  • HANA Audit – Change Events – Full-width table of the 500 most recent HANA user/role/privilege/password/DDL actions with Operator, Target, Category, Action, Status, HANA Host (the HANA host that wrote the audit record) and Client Host (the host name of the client that ran the action, src_host; empty when the record names none). Up to build 377 the table had one Host column, which showed the client’s host name.
  • Windows – Account & Group Modifications – Full-width table of the 500 most recent Windows Security events across all 15 canonical account/group EventCodes, with human-readable Description column derived from EventCode.
  • Linux – Sudo & Command Activity – Full-width table of the 500 most recent sudo commands + useradd/usermod/userdel/groupadd/groupmod/groupdel/passwd activity, with Operator (extracted from sudo prefix or PAM (user) pattern) and Command.
  • Recent Privileged Changes (Compliance Focus) – Table (left half of the bottom row) of the 500 most recent events in the highest-risk subset: HANA Permission Grants + User Creations + Audit Policy changes; Windows account creation/enable/password-reset + local-group additions; Linux useradd / usermod / userdel / visudo activity. This is the “who gave themselves or others more access” report.
  • Recent After-Hours Changes (Outside Business Hours) – Table (right half of the bottom row) of the 500 most recent change events with is_after_hours=1. This is the “who was working outside the change window” report – high compliance value.

docs.title: Where the Data Comes From
docs.text:
Sources span the three change surfaces: sap:hana:audit (user/role/privilege/DDL changes), XmlWinEventLog (account and group changes) and the Linux family (linux_messages_syslog, linux_secure, linux:sudolog, linux:cron, linux:warn, linux:slapd, plus legacy syslog).

  • Summary-backed panels — the KPIs, sparklines, activity chart, category donut and operator table read the logserv_compliance_rollup KV Store collection: metric main carries an hourly grain over (change source, category, operator), and metrics userchg, permgrant and password pre-compute their KPIs’ exact filters per hour. After-hours is not stored: the After-Hours KPI and sparkline derive it when you view the dashboard, from each hourly bucket, in your time zone — the same rule the raw After-Hours table applies to each event, so the two agree. (In a time zone with a half-hour offset, such as India at UTC+05:30, an hour that straddles 08:00 or 19:00 is judged by its start.) Populated at minute :12 of every hour by logserv_compliance_aggregate.
  • Live panels — the five audit-trail tables (HANA, Windows, Linux, Privileged Changes, After-Hours) are per-event listings dispatched against the raw events at view time (capped at the 500 most recent matches each) — deliberately raw, so the compliance record shows actual events rather than summaries.

Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search); a fresh install seeds the last 30 days from Settings → Dashboard Data → Run backfill. The global Cloud dropdown filters the summaries through the cloud_provider dimension stored in every rollup row. Full schedule and freshness reference: Performance & Data Freshness.

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
• Rows in the Privileged Changes table with unfamiliar operators – The “headline” compliance question. A permission grant or group-addition you don’t recognize is the first thing to investigate.
  • After-Hours activity on business days – The After-Hours table surfaces all outside-window activity. Weekend entries are often planned maintenance; weekday late-night or early-morning entries warrant a check against your change tickets.
  • Single operator dominating the Operators by Change Count table – One identity generating most changes can be legitimate (an admin performing a large rollout) or concerning (an account being abused). The source prefix tells you which system to look at first.
  • Category-mix drift – If the Change Events by Category donut suddenly shows a large “Permission Grant” slice where it’s historically been minor, someone has been handing out privileges. Check the HANA Audit table for details.
  • Source asymmetry – The stacked column should show all three sources over time. If one source goes silent, it’s likely a logging-pipeline issue rather than “no changes happened”. Correlate with Data Pipeline Overview.
  • Linux sudo commands starting with useradd/usermod/visudo/passwd – These are the Linux equivalent of admin changes; they show up in both the Linux table and the Privileged Changes table for visibility.

Compliance-focused exception: no row drill-downs on the After-Hours and Privileged Changes tables

Two compliance-focused tables on this dashboard intentionally have no row drill-downs — the After-Hours Changes and Recent Privileged Changes tables. Clicking through to raw events from a compliance audit-trail report would pollute the trail with the reviewer’s own search activity in subsequent compliance reports. Per-source operational tables on the same dashboard (HANA Audit, Windows Account & Group Modifications, Linux Sudo & Command Activity) DO get drill-downs.

docs.title: Why This Dashboard Matters
docs.text: Authentication failures are usually investigated one layer at a time – someone looks at HANA audit logs, then switches to Windows Event Log, then opens the SAP services dashboard. An attacker who probes multiple layers at once is therefore hard to spot. Cross-Stack Authentication unifies the failure signal across the three layers that matter in an SAP landscape – SAP sapstartsrv, HANA audit, and Windows Security Event Log – so that a single pane shows the total, the per-layer split, and the source IPs and users in common across layers. Use it as the first stop when you suspect credential-based attacks or widespread misconfiguration after a password rotation.

docs.title: Panels
docs.text:
The title row carries the app-wide Cloud Provider picker (All / aws / azure / gcp); any setting other than All scopes every panel below to that ingest channel.

  • Total Auth Failures – Aggregate failed authentication count across all three layers
  • SAP Auth Failures – Count of sapstartsrv authentication failures
  • HANA Auth Failures – Count of HANA audit events where the connection/authentication was rejected
  • Windows Auth Failures – Count of Windows Security-channel events (sourcetype XmlWinEventLog) where the CIM action field is failure (the classification comes from the Splunk Add-on for Windows on the search-head tier)
  • Auth Failures Over Time by Layer – Stacked column chart showing totals per layer over time (SAP / HANA / Windows) so correlated spikes across layers are visible at a glance
  • Users by Auth Failures – Table of failing usernames ranked by failure count, summed across all three layers (paginated)
  • Auth Failure Source IPs – Table of source IPs ranked by failure count, showing how many layers each IP hit and which ones, plus last-seen time (paginated); row drilldown opens that IP’s full cross-stack auth history in Search
  • HANA Auth Activity by User – Table of HANA users across ALL authentication activity (successes included), showing total events, distinct action types, failure count, risk level, and last-seen time, sorted by failures; row drilldown opens that user’s full HANA auth log
  • Recent Windows Auth Failures – Table of the most recent Windows failure events (up to 200) with user, event signature, source IP, logon type, and host; row drilldown opens Host Details for that host
  • Recent SAP Auth Failures – Table of the most recent sapstartsrv failed-auth events (up to 200) with user, remote IP, source location, and host; row drilldown opens Host Details for that host

docs.title: Where the Data Comes From
docs.text:
• Summary-backed panels read the logserv_xstack_auth_rollup KV Store collection — metric fail carries the cross-source authentication-failure grain over (layer, failed user) spanning sap:sapstartsrv, sap:hana:audit and XmlWinEventLog; metric failip the per-source-IP failure facts (layers hit, last seen); metric hanauser the full HANA authentication population (successes included) per user/action/status/risk level. Populated at minute :15 of every hour by logserv_xstack_auth_aggregate.
  • Live panels — the Windows events and SAP authentication tables are per-event listings dispatched against the raw events at view time, capped at the 200 most recent matches each.

Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search); a fresh install seeds the last 30 days from Settings → Dashboard Data → Run backfill. The global Cloud dropdown filters the summaries through the cloud_provider dimension stored in every rollup row. Full schedule and freshness reference: Performance & Data Freshness.

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
• Correlated spikes across layers – If the stacked Auth Failures Over Time chart shows all three layers ramping simultaneously, that’s almost always a network-level attack (password spray, credential stuffing) rather than a local misconfiguration. Investigate source IPs immediately.
  • Single source IP across layers – The Auth Failure Source IPs table makes it obvious when one IP is failing against SAP, HANA, AND Windows. That’s the hallmark of a targeted attack rather than an expired-password incident.
  • High user failure count concentrated on service accounts – Service accounts (sapadm, sapservice accounts, DBADMIN-style) with large failure counts suggest either a recently rotated password that wasn’t updated downstream, or an attacker trying to abuse a high-privilege account.
  • Asymmetry between layers – Many HANA failures but zero SAP / Windows failures usually indicates an application-layer issue (bad connection string, expired JDBC cert). Asymmetry the other way (many Windows failures, no HANA failures) often points to a domain-level issue.
  • After a password rotation – Expect a short burst of failures across one or more layers immediately after a change. If the burst persists beyond the rotation window, some downstream system is still using the old credential.

docs.title: Why This Dashboard Matters
docs.text: Firewall drops, proxy traffic, and DNS queries are three different lenses on the same underlying question: what is crossing the network boundary and should it be there? Each lens lives on its own operational dashboard (Linux, Proxy Analytics, DNS Analytics), but an attacker rarely limits themselves to a single surface – a compromised host often shows up in multiple signals simultaneously, and that correlation is where the security value lives. Network Perimeter synthesizes the three sources into a single view: rejected traffic (firewall drops at the host and in transit), outbound flow (proxy), and resolution activity (DNS), with a dedicated cross-source panel that ranks hosts by combined suspicious-signal score. Use it as the first stop for “is our network perimeter healthy and clean?”

docs.title: Panels
docs.text:
The title row carries the app-wide Cloud Provider picker (All / aws / azure / gcp). Every panel on this dashboard is scoped by it; leave it on All unless you are deliberately isolating one ingest channel.

  • Firewall Drops at Host – Count of kernel firewall IN_DROP events from linux_secure: packets addressed to the host itself, dropped by its INPUT chain
  • Firewall Drops in Transit – Count of kernel firewall FWD_DROP events: packets a host was routing on to another system, dropped by its FORWARD chain. Only hosts that forward traffic, such as VPN or IPsec gateways, log these. Read from the Linux dashboard’s summary data, so it shows 0, or undercounts, for any period the Linux rollup has not summarised: its aggregation turned off, or those days not backfilled. The row to rebuild in Settings → Dashboard Data is Linux System & Security / Network Perimeter
  • Proxy Requests – Count of HTTP requests handled by Squid
  • DNS Queries – Count of DNS queries from isc:bind:query
  • Beaconing Domains (red) – Domains exhibiting periodic query patterns (low variance in inter-query interval) – candidate C2 channels. Beaconing is detected per UTC calendar day (a domain’s inter-query gaps are analysed within each UTC day, whatever timezone you view the dashboard in), and the KPI is the sum of each day’s distinct beaconing-domain count over the selected range – a domain beaconing every day for a week counts 7. Its sparkline has one point per UTC day, and hovering a point shows that UTC date; a UTC day that has not ended yet is drawn at 0 and labelled not yet computed. The beaconing panels are refreshed by a daily scheduled search (00:30 search-head local time), so they can lag up to 24 h; the other panels on this dashboard refresh hourly
  • Denied Requests (orange when non-zero) – Count of proxy requests with status=403 or vendor_action="TCP_DENIED"; click to drill down
  • Outbound Bandwidth – sum(bytes_out) across all proxy requests, formatted KB/MB/GB
  • Perimeter Activity Over Time – Full-width stacked column chart showing counts of all three sources over time on a single timeline; simultaneous spikes across two or three series are the correlation signal to watch for. Its firewall series is Firewall Drops at Host; drops in transit are not charted here.
  • Blocked Source IPs – Every source IP in the firewall log, ranked by Total (paginated) and split into At Host and In Transit / Other, with unique target count and protocols seen; row drilldown to the matching events

  • Blocked Destination Ports – All destination ports targeted by firewall traffic, grouped by port + protocol, ranked by Total (paginated) and split the same way

    Both Blocked tables count every firewall event carrying a source IP / destination port. At Host is the IN_DROP events among them; In Transit / Other is the rest: nearly all FWD_DROP, plus any other firewall line logged with a source or port. ICMP carries no destination port, so ICMP drops appear in Blocked Source IPs but not in Blocked Destination Ports. - Firewall Drops at Host by Protocol – Stacked column showing IN_DROP events over time (drops at the host, INPUT chain) split by TCP / UDP / ICMP. Protocol shifts are often the clearest signal (ICMP spikes = ping flood / recon; UDP spikes = DNS amplification / port scan; TCP spikes = SYN-style port scan) - Proxy Denied Traffic Over Time – Column chart of denied proxy requests over time – the outbound complement to the firewall drops - Outbound Domains by Volume & Bytes – All destination domains receiving outbound traffic, ranked by bytes (paginated), with request count and unique client count. Row drilldown opens the events for that domain. - DNS Query Type Distribution – Donut of query-type mix (A / AAAA / PTR / TXT / MX / other). High TXT or MX volume from non-mail hosts is a DNS-tunneling / exfiltration indicator. - Queried Domains – Table (right of the query-type donut) of all queried domains ranked by query count, with unique-client count and per-domain %TXT / %MX ratios for quick anomaly spotting. Row drilldown opens DNS query events for that domain. - Suspicious Activity Indicator – Full-width cross-source table of internal hosts appearing in both beaconing DNS queries and denied proxy requests, ranked by signal score (beacon_domains × 3 + denied_requests). Columns: Host, Beaconing Domains, Beaconing Queries, Denied Proxy Requests, Signal Score. Row drilldown opens the Host Details dashboard for that host (its full cross-sourcetype activity), carrying the current time range.

docs.title: Where the Data Comes From
docs.text:
This dashboard synthesises three perimeter sources, all summary-backed:

  • logserv_perimeter_rollup (populated at minute :16 of every hour by logserv_perimeter_aggregate) carries seven metrics: fw (firewall actions/sources/ports — the SRC= / DST= / DPT= / PROTO= fields are extracted from the raw linux_secure events at aggregation time), proxy + proxydom (Squid request/denied/bandwidth counts and per-domain traffic), dnscount + dnstype + dnsq (DNS query volume, types, and per-query/source counts over the tag=dns events), and activity (the combined activity chart’s classification).
  • Firewall Drops in Transit reads the Linux dashboard’s logserv_linux_rollup collection (metric kernel, the kernel tag of every linux_secure line per hour), because the perimeter fw metric does not tell a FWD_DROP line from other firewall lines. For any period that rollup has not summarised (its aggregation turned off, or those days not backfilled) it shows 0 or undercounts. The row to rebuild in Settings → Dashboard Data is Linux System & Security / Network Perimeter.
  • The beaconing panels read the daily collections: logserv_beaconing_rollup (00:30) for the KPI and logserv_beaconing_detail_rollup (00:32, metrics qs + denied) for the suspicious activity detail — daily cadence because the gap-variance detection needs a day of inter-arrival history, so these panels update once per day rather than hourly.

Summary-backed panels switch automatically to their exact raw-equivalent search when the selected window is shorter than 90 minutes, so sub-hour investigation stays real-time. The collection keeps 365 days of hourly history (trimmed by a daily retention search); a fresh install seeds the last 30 days from Settings → Dashboard Data → Run backfill. The global Cloud dropdown filters the summaries through the cloud_provider dimension stored in every rollup row. Full schedule and freshness reference: Performance & Data Freshness.

docs.title: What to Look For
docs.text:
• Correlated spikes across sources – The Perimeter Activity Over Time chart is the quickest read on “is something happening right now?” Watch for days when two or three of the series spike together – that’s usually an active event (port scan, active C2, exfiltration window) rather than baseline drift.
  • Protocol shifts in firewall drops – The protocol chart of drops at the host is more diagnostic than raw drop counts. A normally TCP-heavy mix suddenly showing large UDP or ICMP bands signals a different attacker technique.
  • Blocked Source IPs concentration – A single source IP generating the overwhelming majority of drops is either a persistent attacker or a misconfigured internal host. Either way, the action is the same: investigate that specific IP.
  • Drops in transit – FWD_DROP comes only from hosts that route traffic, such as VPN or IPsec gateways. On a gateway it is traffic the forwarding policy does not allow, often a monitoring or discovery job probing the systems behind the gateway, and it can outnumber the drops at the host many times over. Use the In Transit / Other column of Blocked Source IPs to find the source, then allow its traffic or stop the job. Drops in transit on a host that should not route at all mean IP forwarding is switched on there.
  • TXT-heavy queries to a single domain – A domain in Queried Domains with a high %TXT ratio is a DNS-tunneling pattern. Cross-reference the Suspicious Activity Indicator to see which hosts are issuing those queries.
  • Hosts in the Suspicious Activity table – Any non-empty row here is worth investigating. A host showing up in both beaconing DNS and denied proxy is strong evidence of compromise – the DNS lookups suggest malware C2, and the denied proxy requests suggest the same malware trying to reach blocked destinations.
  • Outbound Bandwidth spikes – A sudden rise in the Outbound Bandwidth KPI that isn’t matched by a proportional rise in Proxy Requests means individual transfers are getting larger – often the signature of an exfiltration event.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
Splunk platform versions 9.4.3 and later CIM 5.0.0 and later (per app.manifest) Supported OS for data collection Platform independent Vendor products SAP LogServ for SAP ECS in Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP) Published App artifact The full-LLM build variant — the free-form LLM path is present but inert until an LLM provider credential is configured; predefined prompts + MCP dispatch work with no credential (see Build Variants) AI Assistant prerequisite Splunk MCP Server (Splunkbase App 7931) v1.0.3 or later — no upper bound since App build 393 (2.0.0 the newest verified); v1.1.0+ recommended — on the search head where the LogServ App is installed AWS ingest The Splunk Add-on for AWS (SQS-Based S3 inputs) on the Heavy Forwarders; the Data TA’s AWS S3 Direct screen accepts 8.1.0 and later, with no upper bound Azure ingest A dedicated first-party add-on — Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on Azure (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_azure), installed per Heavy Forwarder GCP ingest A dedicated first-party add-on — Splunk TA for SAP LogServ on GCP (splunk_ta_sap_logserv_gcp), installed per Heavy Forwarder

v0.1.2 continues the v0.1.1 line

v0.1.2 is the active LLM-capable line and carries everything listed under Version 0.1.1 below — the dashboard-performance data layer (tstats + KV-Store rollups, the backfill panel, staggered schedules), the Azure and GCP ingest add-ons, the LogServ Data Doctor, the Environment Topology work, and the full LLM-driven AI Assistant. The published App artifact is the full-LLM build variant, so the free-form path is present and becomes active once an LLM provider credential is configured; the compile-time templates-only variant of the same source remains available for deployments where that restriction must not be reversible (see Build Variants). Entries for this release are added as work lands.

docs.title: The Audit Log’s user filter shows each name once (build 394)
docs.text:
• With User contains set, Settings → AI Assistant → Audit Log showed each name twice in the User column (for example adminadmin). The filter makes Splunk extract user from the event to apply it, and the viewer’s spath then added the same value again. The viewer now reads user from the event’s JSON after spath, as it already did for category, so the column shows the name once with or without the filter.

After upgrading: nothing to rebuild, and no acknowledgement is asked again.

docs.title: A newer Splunk MCP Server is no longer refused (build 393)
docs.text:
• The AI Assistant runs against any Splunk MCP Server from v1.0.3 up. It used to refuse a version at or above an upper bound it had not been tested against (v3.0.0 since build 335), replacing the chat with an Uncertified version card. That bound is gone; the v1.0.3 floor (CVE-2026-20205) stays. A version reported in two parts, such as 3.0, now reads as 3.0.0; it used to be refused as too old. The newest version verified is 2.0.0 (the handshake, tools/list and tools/call); if a later version changed the protocol the AI Assistant depends on, that would show as failing tool calls in the chat rather than as a refusal to start.

After upgrading: nothing to rebuild, and no acknowledgement is asked again.

docs.title: Audit events go where the settings in place when they were posted send them, and the dialog names both providers (build 392)
docs.text:
• An audit event posted on its own goes where the audit settings in place at that moment send it. That covers the Settings page’s acknowledgement events, which are posted just before the save. Until now the forwarder setting was read only after the event’s local write, so that save could decide, while the event was being written, whether the event was also sent to the off-host forwarder. Now a Yes that turns forwarding off is also sent to the forwarder being turned off (an attempt with the forwarder settings the page has applied), and if that send fails, its failure record goes to the event’s audit index, even when the same save renames the index.
  • On a re-ask whose save also changes the LLM provider, the enablement dialog names both: the provider in effect, which a No keeps, and the one the save changes it to, which a Yes saves.
  • The build-time tests are stricter. The legal-text test reads the code with its comments removed and pins each acknowledgement event’s fields, the call that posts it, and the awaited record of each answer in its own store. The audit-writer test checks where an event goes when the settings change while it is being written.

After upgrading: nothing to rebuild, and no acknowledgement is asked again: the legal texts and their versions are unchanged.

docs.title: The audit-forwarding Yes is logged even when the save after it fails (build 391)
docs.text:
• The audit-forwarding acknowledgement’s audit event is posted as soon as the answer is recorded, for a Yes as for a No. A Yes’s event used to wait for the save, so a Yes followed by a failed save could leave the Yes recorded with no audit event, and the retry did not always ask again.
  • On a re-ask, the enablement dialog names the provider in effect, the one a No keeps; it named the provider selected on the page. When the AI Assistant is being turned on, it still names the page’s provider.
  • The build-time legal-text test pins both, and pins the Settings page’s busy state more tightly: set before the turn-off write, released when that write fails, held until the No is recorded. Its provider checks skip // comment lines. Also: a code-style fix and comment fixes.

After upgrading: nothing to rebuild, and no acknowledgement is asked again: the legal texts and their versions are unchanged.

docs.title: The Settings page waits for a No to be recorded, and the audit-forwarding dialog shows its errors (build 390)
docs.text:
• A No that turns the AI Assistant off keeps the Settings page busy until the No is recorded (the Save button reads Saving…); the page could be used again a moment too early.
  • The audit-forwarding dialog closes when its answer cannot be recorded, or when the save after a Yes fails, so the error shows on the page; it appeared behind the dialog.
  • A No’s audit event records the provider in effect, for both acknowledgements; it recorded the provider selected on the page, which a No does not save.
  • The build-time legal-text test pins all three. Also: comment fixes.

After upgrading: nothing to rebuild, and no acknowledgement is asked again: the legal texts and their versions are unchanged.

docs.title: The enablement dialog closes once the AI Assistant is off (build 389)
docs.text:
• No turn-on wording during a No. When a No turns the AI Assistant off, the dialog now closes as soon as that is done, before the No is recorded; until now it showed the turn-on wording and buttons for that moment.
  • An answer that cannot be recorded closes the dialog, so the error shows on the page; it used to appear behind the dialog.
  • The build-time legal-text test pins both. Also: comment fixes.

After upgrading: nothing to rebuild, and no acknowledgement is asked again: the legal texts and their versions are unchanged.

docs.title: Declining the AI Assistant terms turns the AI Assistant off (build 388)
docs.text:
• A No now does what the terms say. The enablement acknowledgement ends by saying that if Customer does not accept, the AI Assistant feature will remain disabled. That held when an admin was turning the AI Assistant on. When it was already on and the terms’ version rose, a No only cancelled that save: the AI Assistant stayed on, and the next save went through without asking. Now a No in that case turns the AI Assistant off. Only the Enable AI Assistant setting changes - nothing else in that save is applied - and it is written before the No is recorded, so if the write fails, the question is asked again at the next save. The dialog says so before the click, and its No button reads I do not accept (record No and turn off).
  • The enablement acknowledgement is at version 3. Its closing sentence now says the AI Assistant feature will then remain disabled or, if it is already enabled, be disabled. A deployment that runs with the AI Assistant enabled is asked once to accept it, at the next Save Defaults; coming from build 386 or earlier, that is the only time (build 387, which raised it to version 2, was not released).
  • The build-time legal-text test pins the version-3 text and the code that carries it out: the turn-off before the No is recorded, the early returns that stop a failed turn-off from being recorded and a declined save from going on, and the dialog’s wording on the re-ask.
  • Also: the Settings page’s message when an answer cannot be recorded no longer repeats itself, and the acknowledgement code’s comments no longer describe the configuration-file write used before build 240.

After upgrading: nothing to rebuild. With the AI Assistant enabled, expect the enablement acknowledgement once, at the next Save Defaults; answering No turns the AI Assistant off.

docs.title: The acknowledgements say where an answer is recorded (build 387)
docs.text:
• The AI Assistant enablement acknowledgement is at version 2. Clause 7 of its text said the administrator’s answer is recorded “via the standard Splunk telemetry endpoint”. The answer is recorded as an event in the AI Assistant audit log, with the administrator’s account name, network address and a timestamp, and, since build 240, stored with the acknowledged version in the KV Store; the clause now says so. Because the wording changed, its version rose from 1 to 2: on a deployment where the AI Assistant is enabled, the next admin who saves the AI Assistant’s General settings (Save Defaults) is asked once to accept the corrected text. Turning the AI Assistant on asks every time, as before.
  • The note under both acknowledgements (outside their legal text) and the Settings page’s message when an answer cannot be recorded named the same telemetry endpoint. The note now names the audit log and the KV Store, and the message names the KV Store, the write that failed.
  • The build-time legal-text test pins the enablement text at version 2 and fails if either acknowledgement, or the Settings page, mentions the telemetry endpoint again.

After upgrading: nothing to rebuild. With the AI Assistant enabled, expect the enablement acknowledgement once, at the next Save Defaults; with audit forwarding off, also the audit-log integrity acknowledgement, unless build 386’s version 2 was already answered.

docs.title: The audit-log integrity acknowledgement names the audit index correctly (build 386)
docs.text:
• The forwarder-disabled acknowledgement is at version 2. Its text named the audit index ai_assistant_audit, the index’s name before it was renamed logserv_ai_assistant_audit; it now reads the AI Assistant audit index (logserv_ai_assistant_audit, or the index set in Settings), so it stays correct where an admin named another index. Because the wording changed, its version rose from 1 to 2: on a deployment that runs with audit forwarding off, the next admin who saves the AI Assistant’s General settings (Save Defaults) is asked once to acknowledge the corrected text. With forwarding on nothing changes, and the AI Assistant enablement acknowledgement is unchanged.
  • A build-time test pins each acknowledgement text to its version. The SHA-256 of each text (the value its audit event records as disclaimerHash) must match the latest entry of that text’s revision history in the test, whose version must equal the optInVersion in ai_assistant_acks.conf, so a changed wording fails the build until it is recorded there as a new revision.
  • Documentation. The add-ons’ urllib3 1.26.20 and the seven advisories scanners report against it are analysed in Third-Party Software Licenses: none affects the add-ons as shipped. The AI Assistant Settings page of this documentation now says an acknowledgement is recorded once per deployment.
  • Comment fixes (the old index name in four source comments, Count / hr in two collections.conf comments, one audit-writer comment) and more build-time tests of the Data Doctor report’s author marker (it is added once, and an empty or unknown author reads an unknown user).

After upgrading: nothing to rebuild. With audit forwarding off, expect the acknowledgement once, at the next Save Defaults in the AI Assistant’s General settings.

docs.title: The audit warning names both capabilities Splunk accepts, and a re-downloaded Data Doctor report marks its author everywhere (build 385)
docs.text:
• The AI Assistant’s audit warning names both capabilities. Splunk accepts the browser’s audit writes (receivers/simple) from a user who holds edit_tcp or edit_log_alert_event, and Splunk’s default power role holds edit_log_alert_event, so power users have been audited all along; only users whose sole role is user are refused. The warning (HTTP 403, or HTTP 401 after a reload) now names edit_log_alert_event, the narrower one to grant, and edit_tcp, and says Splunk’s default user role has neither; it no longer says power users lack them. See Audit Log.
  • A re-downloaded Data Doctor report marks its author everywhere. Build 384 marked the name on the cover page only; the environment-fingerprint section’s Generated by, the machine-readable appendix and the JSON copy now show <name> (name not verified) too.
  • The ingest-cutoff sentence gives the date first. The Data Doctor now says a range ends before the ingest cutoff of <date> (recorded as supplied by <name> (name not verified)), so the date no longer reads as the time the cutoff was supplied.
  • The Dashboard Data upgrade note names every panel a Backfill without the Clear inflates. Activity by SID / Instance on Work Process Performance counts the upgraded hours twice as well, and its WP Categories column counts each renamed component twice.
  • Comment and description fixes in ai_assistant_acks.conf, collections.conf, default.meta and savedsearches.conf (the topology detail search’s description names the node’s Count / hr chart).

After upgrading: nothing to rebuild.

docs.title: Dashboard data writable by admins only, writer searches run as the requesting user, and two Data Doctor fixes (build 384)
docs.text:
The App’s KV Store collections that hold dashboard data - the 24 rollups, the five Environment Topology collections and the Data Doctor’s platform snapshot - were writable by every role, so any signed-in user could alter or delete what the dashboards show through Splunk’s REST API. They are now writable by the admin, sc_admin and sc_subadmin roles only; every role can still read them. Their scheduled searches run as Splunk’s system user and the Settings → Dashboard Data backfill as the signed-in admin, so neither changes. Six collections stay writable by every role because ordinary users write them by design: the four per-user preferences (topology layouts, the default layout, the active layout mode, the dashboard refresh interval) and the Data Doctor’s saved reports and supplied ingest configuration.

  • Saved searches that write run as the requesting user. The 91 saved searches that write with outputlookup (the aggregate, backfill and retention searches of the rollups and topology collections, the Data Doctor’s platform-snapshot and report-retention searches, and the two ES feeds) now set dispatchAs = user. A user who starts one through Splunk’s REST API (saved/searches/<name>/dispatch) runs it with their own permissions, so a non-admin can no longer run a retention or a backfill that overwrites dashboard data. Their schedules run as before.
  • A stored refresh interval must be one the picker offers. The refresh-interval collection is writable by every role, so another user could store a one-second interval in your row and make every panel re-run each second; a stored value other than Never, 30s, 1m, 5m, 15m, 30m or 1hr is now ignored.
  • The Data Doctor says a supplier name is not verified. The name on a saved report and on a supplied ingest configuration is the one the browser sent, so the Data Doctor now shows it as (name not verified): the saved reports’ column reads By (not verified), and a re-downloaded saved report marks the name on its cover page (its environment-fingerprint section, appendix and JSON copy still show the name as stored). The page’s note on saved reports no longer says every App collection is writable by every user. The platform snapshot’s provenance line now reads recorded by the hourly platform snapshot, a collection only Splunk administrators can write.

After upgrading: nothing to rebuild. A metadata/local.meta stanza for one of these collections keeps its own ACL; remove it to take the new one. A scheduled search of your own that writes into one of these collections and is owned by a non-admin user stops writing.

docs.title: AI Assistant settings writable by admins only, a warning when audit events are not written, and SAP’s names for the trace components (build 383)
docs.text:
After upgrading, rebuild one row in Settings → Dashboard Data, Work Process Performance / ABAP Operations, because the trace-component names it stores have changed: Clear then Backfill it, or use the narrower repair at the end of this entry, which keeps the row’s older history. The page shows an upgrade note that names the row; see After upgrading below and Upgrading.

AI Assistant security

  • Only admins can change the AI Assistant’s settings. Its settings, its legal acknowledgements and its discovered-model cache live in three KV Store collections (logserv_ai_assistant_settings, logserv_ai_assistant_acks, logserv_ai_models) that every role could write. A signed-in user without admin rights could therefore change, through Splunk’s REST API, where an admin’s browser sends the audit forwarder’s HEC token (the forwarder URL) and the MCP bearer token (the MCP server URL), or the privacy tier. The three collections are now writable by the admin, sc_admin and sc_subadmin roles only; every role can still read them. The writes other users’ pages used to make there (a one-time move of conf-file values at page load, the model list’s refresh) were best-effort; they are now refused, quietly, and an admin’s page makes them.

AI Assistant audit log

  • A warning when audit events are not written. The browser writes the AI Assistant’s audit events to logserv_ai_assistant_audit through Splunk’s receivers/simple endpoint, as the signed-in user, and that needs the edit_tcp or the edit_log_alert_event capability, which Splunk Enterprise’s default admin and power roles hold and user does not (this entry first said admin only). A refused write used to be dropped with a line in the browser console, so the activity of users without either capability went unaudited without a sign. While writes fail, the chat panel now shows an amber warning - on HTTP 403 it names edit_tcp; on HTTP 401, which usually means the Splunk Web session has ended, it asks for a reload first - and the session’s audit list notes from when its events may be missing from the index. Which capability to grant, and what each allows, is in Audit Log.
  • The batch still buffered when a tab closes is sent. It went out as a browser beacon, which cannot carry Splunk Web’s CSRF header and was refused for every user; it is now a keep-alive request with the header, carrying the newest events that fit in 60 KB. Like every audit write, it still needs edit_tcp or edit_log_alert_event.
  • The audit index default is logserv_ai_assistant_audit in the App’s configuration fallbacks and the Audit Log viewer, which still named the retired ai_assistant_audit. The legal text of the forwarder acknowledgement still names it (corrected in build 386, as version 2); changing that text would ask an admin to accept it again (it is accepted once per deployment, not per admin).

SAP’s names for the work process trace components

  • The letter that starts each work process trace (dev_w*) line names SAP’s trace component, and ten of the App’s names change. Seven were wrong: C is the database-specific layer (C = Database (DBSL), not Communication), X extended memory (not RFC / CPIC), M the task handler (not memory management), S spool (not SQL / statistics), T the debug system (not the task handler), D the Diag processor (not the dispatcher), and N security - SNC, SSF, logon tickets (not the network interface); R reads R = Rolling and O is below. E (enqueue), G (language support), H (ICF / HTTP), I (IPC), J (VM container), L (background), P (paging) and W (WebGUI / ITS) get names, O and V, which SAP’s public lists do not name, are named from their lines (program buffer / PXA, coverage analyzer), and Q, which is not a trace component, reads Q = Other. The names come from SAP Help’s “Trace Components” list and SAP Note 112. They appear in wp_category_name and in the Work Process Performance, ABAP Operations and Host Details panels; searches, alerts or dashboards of your own that filter on the old wp_category_name values need the new ones.

Environment Topology

  • The partner donuts and the hourly chart say what they count. A system’s “Partners calling this system” and “Partners this system calls” donuts name their unit from that side’s edge types - calls, connections (RFC and SAP Router edges count connections), or calls + connections, with “total” under a mixed donut’s centre - and the node’s hourly chart reads Count / hr, as the Live Activity chart does.

AI Assistant

  • The sourcetype reference names fields that exist. The logserv_sourcetype_metadata_lookup the AI Assistant can read listed, for 30 of its 35 sourcetypes, fields the sourcetype does not have (sap_inst, severity and msg on the ABAP sourcetypes, for example), and 17 of its example searches returned nothing. Every row now names fields that the App, the Data TA or - for the Windows and Linux rows - Splunk’s Windows and *nix add-ons produce, and an example search that runs; the four Windows rows use the real sourcetype, XmlWinEventLog, and name their channel in source.

After upgrading (from build 379): in Settings → Dashboard Data, note the History of Work Process Performance / ABAP Operations, click Clear, then its own Backfill over a window that covers that history (the 365-day preset reaches as far as the rollup keeps it). Without the Clear, rows stored under the old names stay beside the new ones, and the Work Process Performance totals, function, category and Activity by SID / Instance panels and the ABAP Operations category pie count those hours twice (the WP Categories column counts each renamed component twice). Keep the backfill clear of 00:34–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:34–02:36 search-head time. Coming from build 378 or earlier, run the build-379 backfills below too.

A narrower repair that keeps older history. The Clear removes everything the row holds - the dispatcher, ICM and ABAP Operations panels’ history too, although their stored values did not change - and a Backfill brings back only what your index still holds raw events for. To keep the older history, after the upgrade delete only the trace-component rows (metric wp) from W onward, where W is the first UTC day whose raw events your index still holds in full (as in the build-378 entry’s narrower repair, epoch seconds of that UTC midnight), with one REST call on the search head’s management port and an admin account, clear of the nightly retention window (the same call with -X GET in place of -X DELETE returns the rows it would delete - at most 50,000 by default, so it shows what the query matches, not how many; check that first, since a DELETE without its query empties the whole collection):

curl -k -u admin -G -X DELETE   "https://<search-head>:8089/servicesNS/nobody/splunk_app_sap_logserv/storage/collections/data/logserv_wp_perf_rollup"   --data-urlencode 'query={"metric":"wp","bucket_ts":{"$gte":<W>}}'

Then Backfill the row with its own Backfill over a custom range from W to today. The Backfill rewrites the row’s other rows in that range under the keys they already have, so nothing is counted twice; trace-component rows older than W keep their old names. If you cannot reach the management port (on Splunk Cloud it must first be opened for you), use the Clear instead.

docs.title: Host Details shows the work processes’ trace components, and the topology inventory takes each host’s most recent SID (build 379)
docs.text:
This build changes no key a rollup stores. After upgrading, click Backfill, without Clear, on two rows in Settings → Dashboard Data; see After upgrading at the end of this entry and Upgrading.

Host Details

  • ABAP Work Process Trace Components replaces ABAP Work Process Mix. The old panel grouped the work process trace (dev_w*) by a work process type the logs do not record, so it never showed. The new one counts the lines by their trace component: the letter each line starts with, named the way wp_category_name names it (for example B = Database Interface; a letter without a name shows as <letter> = Other).

Environment Topology

  • A host or address seen under two SAP systems takes its most recent one. The host-to-SID inventory recorded an endpoint only in an hour whose log lines all named one SID, and a row once written stayed, so an endpoint whose lines named two systems kept the SID of its last single-system hour, possibly a stale one, and one that had never had such an hour had no row. It now records each endpoint under the SID of its newest hour of activity; when that hour names two, the one with more events; an exact tie writes nothing and keeps the previous row. Endpoints left unattributed before can now fold into a system’s node, and an address that serves two systems at once is drawn under the one that logs more.
  • The totals that add up different edge types say so: Total calls + connections, Inbound calls + connections and Outbound calls + connections (RFC and SAP Router edges count connections, not calls), and the Live Activity table’s column reads Count.

Smaller changes

  • The AI Assistant’s data-model hint names the fields the ABAP sourcetypes extract (sap_instance, the dispatcher’s dp_severity, dp_function and dp_reason, the work process’s wp_function, the enqueue server’s enq_function) instead of sap_inst, severity, message and error_code, which none of them extracts; sap:saphostexec and sap:sapstartsrv get a line of their own.
  • The upgrade hint on Settings → Dashboard Data no longer speaks of a 30-day backfill window: a Clear discards graph history older than the window you backfill, so pick one that covers it.
  • The documentation explains how to keep the AI Assistant’s audit index to its reviewers: Splunk’s default user role can search every index whose name does not start with _, the audit index among them (Audit Log).

After upgrading (from build 378): in Settings → Dashboard Data, click the row’s own Backfill, without Clear, on Host Role Activity (Host Details), so the trace component panel shows history (the 365-day preset fills all of it), and on Environment Topology (graph), whose inventory always reads the last 30 days whatever window you choose. Use each row’s own button: Run backfill skips rows it considers complete. Coming from build 377 or earlier, the build-378 Clear + Backfill below covers both rows when you run it on this build. Keep the backfills clear of 00:34–00:58, 01:30–01:58 and 02:34–02:36 search-head time.

docs.title: SAP Router and RFC connections in the topology, the HANA audit host, HANA trace lines read by their format, and the SAP client in the ICM trace — rebuild eleven rollups once (build 378)
docs.text:
This build changes values that several rollups store, most of them in the keys the rows are stored under. Rows written before the upgrade keep the old values, so after upgrading eleven rows in Settings → Dashboard Data need one Clear and Backfill; see After upgrading at the end of this entry and Upgrading.

Environment Topology

  • SAP Router is a new integration type. Each router’s CONNECT TO lines become an edge from the router host — drawn as its own square, tagged SAP ROUTER, and never folded into an SAP system even when the same VM runs one — to the address it routed to, with the number of routed connections. A target named <ip>/sapms<SID> is that system’s message server, so its address is attributed to the SID and the edge ends on the system’s circle; targets reached by port or sapgw<NN> stay addresses until another source attributes them. The router’s failed server-side connections that name a target IPv4 address (NiBufReceive S… '<IPv4>' failed) count as the edge’s failed connections; client-side failures and failures that name a host are not counted. Loopback targets (127.0.0.0/8, such as a router’s port-3298 niping self-test) are left out. The edges have their own legend colour and filter checkbox, and the Edge Details pane shows routed and failed connections, the top target services (Operations, counted in routed connections) and the target role mix (Performance). New search-time fields on sap:saprouter: saprouter_target_addr, saprouter_target_ip, saprouter_target_service, saprouter_target_sid, saprouter_target_role (message server, gateway, gateway (secure), dispatcher, SAP Router, niping, other service), saprouter_target_instance and saprouter_fail_target_ip; ports 3298 (niping) and 3299 (SAP Router) carry no instance number. See SAP Router.
  • RFC edges count connections, in the direction they were made. The SAP gateway trace (dev_rd) records connections and their failures, not individual RFC calls. An RFC edge now counts the connections it saw: closed connections to remote gateways (outbound), closed client sessions (inbound) and broken connections, each broken connection once (before, each of its up to three trace lines counted as a call; two broken connections to the same remote gateway count as two). Errors are the broken connections, so an edge never shows more errors than connections, and the Edge Details pane says connections and broken connections where it said calls and errors. A connection made to a system’s gateway is now drawn from the caller to the system; until now every RFC edge pointed away from it. Clients and peers on a loopback address (127.0.0.0/8) are left out, so systems that each log a local client on 127.0.0.1 are not joined through one shared address node. Remote gateway hosts are named by the last hop of an SAP Router route and their short host name. The Operations tab of an RFC edge lists the remote gateway services and client programs, and the Performance tab the mix of connection records — both were empty for RFC edges before. The By app server table names the address of the gateway that recorded each connection; connection records name no local address and are grouped as (not recorded). New fields on sap:abap:gateway: gw_remgw_target, gw_remgw_service, gw_remgw_id, gw_client_ip, gw_client_hostname, gw_client_tp, gw_client_id, rfc_peer_port and rfc_local_port.
  • Saved layouts keep new types switched on. A layout records the integration types that were ticked, so a type added after it was saved used to load unticked. Layouts saved earlier now load with SAP Router enabled; layouts saved from now on also record which types existed, so a type you switch off stays off.
  • The health ring and the Edge Details error rate never exceed 100 %, and an edge whose only records in the window are failures counts as fully failed. HANA Tenant duration figures say that each hdbcons command’s duration is converted to milliseconds from the unit its trace line records.
  • HANA audit edges end on the HANA host that wrote each record (see HANA below), and node errors no longer list ICM sessions as HTTP errors (see ICM below).
  • Web Dispatcher events count toward their system. Web Dispatcher requests now also count toward their host’s node and toward the Hosts and Errors tabs of the system their log path names (a system’s Errors tab may now list Web Dispatcher HTTP 4xx / 5xx kinds; the tab shows the top 20).
